defaults.permitted_development: Across Berkshire, a dropped kerb is normally more of a highways process than a pure planning matter because the work crosses public footway or verge. Planning permission can still enter the picture where the access is onto a classified road, where householder rights do not apply, or where the frontage changes go beyond a simple crossover.

rules.height_rules: Across Berkshire, height is not the main planning test for a dropped kerb, but changes in levels still matter. A scheme can become problematic if raised ground, steep gradients or tall boundary features interfere with safe access.
rules.depth_rules: Across Berkshire, the real depth question is practical rather than formula-based: can a vehicle enter and sit inside the site without blocking the footway? Tight front gardens often fail on that point even before wider design issues are considered.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Berkshire, the highway crossing remains public land, so approval can turn on visibility, drainage, kerb alignment, utilities and street obstacles rather than on the private driveway alone. Front walls, hedges and gate positions often have to be designed as part of the same access package.
rules.roof_rules: Across Berkshire, there is no separate roof rule for a dropped kerb. The practical equivalent is whether the access works also introduce other structures, such as a covered entrance, taller gate piers or retaining features, which need to be assessed on their own terms.
rules.materials_rules: Across Berkshire, materials matter differently here than on a normal householder project. The authority will usually control the kerb and footway construction, while the private driveway behind it should be robust, well-drained and suitable for repeated vehicle loading.

restrictions.conservation_area: A dropped kerb in a conservation area often needs fuller scrutiny if the proposal affects established front boundaries, historic paving or the character of the street.
restrictions.listed_building: A new crossing serving a listed building can need listed building consent where boundary walls, gates, steps, railings or other historic fabric are altered.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions or planning conditions can remove the simpler householder route for access and boundary works, so the planning status should be checked before relying only on highway approval.

rules.permitted_development: In Reading, creating a new vehicular access usually starts with highway consent rather than a normal householder application. Lowering the kerb and strengthening the footway are public-highway works, and planning permission may still be required if the site fronts a classified road, the property is split into flats, or the proposal depends on larger engineering or boundary changes.

rules.height_rules: Dropped-kerb work is controlled more by highway geometry than by a simple height limit. The council will care about levels, gradients and whether boundary features need to come down to maintain visibility.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national planning depth limit, but the access should lead to enough in-curtilage standing space for a vehicle to clear the footway rather than overhang it. Schemes become harder where a car would project onto the pavement or rely on awkward reversing.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary and highway issues usually decide a dropped-kerb application more than any householder rulebook. The authority may object because of sightlines, nearby junctions, parking controls, street furniture or conflicts with utility apparatus.
rules.roof_rules: Roof form is not part of a dropped-kerb assessment, but do not ignore linked structures. If the scheme also adds a canopy, car-port edge, gateway feature or retaining work, those pieces are not automatically covered by the crossing approval.
rules.materials_rules: Materials matter differently here than on a normal householder project. The authority will usually control the kerb and footway construction, while the private driveway behind it should be robust, well-drained and suitable for repeated vehicle loading.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status usually makes a new access more sensitive where it removes historic boundary features or changes a traditional frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be required where dropped-kerb works alter the setting or fabric of a listed building, including curtilage walls and entrance features.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction or an old planning condition can remove normal householder rights for frontage and access changes, even where the dropped kerb itself still needs separate highway consent.

rules.permitted_development: In Slough, creating a new vehicular access usually starts with highway consent rather than a normal householder application. rules.height_rules: A dropped kerb does not have its own building-height rule. What matters is whether the level changes, gradients and any reduction in walls or hedges still produce a safe and workable access.
rules.depth_rules: No fixed national depth rule applies, but the site should be deep enough for a vehicle to stand within the property once it has crossed the footway. If the car would overhang the pavement, the access is far less likely to be acceptable.
rules.boundary_rules: The highway crossing remains public land, so approval can turn on visibility, drainage, kerb alignment, utilities and street obstacles rather than on the private driveway alone. Front walls, hedges and gate positions often have to be designed as part of the same access package.
rules.roof_rules: A dropped kerb has no roof-related permitted development test. The nearest equivalent design issue is whether any linked canopy, gate feature or retaining structure is being added as part of the access works, because those elements are assessed under their own rules.
rules.materials_rules: You do not get a householder right to choose the kerb build-up or footway construction yourself: the highway authority usually specifies the crossing detail. Behind the kerb, use a durable surface and drainage layout that can take vehicle loading without washing water onto the pavement or road.

restrictions.conservation_area: Within a conservation area, access works that disturb original walls, railings, kerb lines or planting often receive a more detailed planning and heritage check.

restrictions.article4_notes: Do not assume the highway licence is the only approval needed: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions can still require a planning application for linked frontage or access works.
